top_level_objectives: Apply VSEPR theory to predict three-dimensional molecular geometry from Lewis structures
Identify and name the five fundamental electron-domain geometries and their modifications by lone pairs
Manipulate electron domains in 3D space to observe minimum-repulsion configurations
Compare VSEPR predictions to real molecular structures and bond angles
Explain how lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, affecting bond angles

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the core concept that electron pairs repel each other and arrange to minimize mutual repulsion. Students observe abstract electron domains moving in space to their lowest-energy configuration.
key_visuals: Central sphere with 2-6 small spheres representing electron domains
Spatial arrangement animating from random to ordered geometry
Energy level indicator (bar chart or color gradient) showing repulsion energy decreasing as pairs spread out
Brief labels identifying 'electron domains' and 'repulsion energy'
student_actions: Watch electron domains automatically arrange themselves in space
Observe energy decrease as domains spread to minimize repulsion
Count the number of domains and identify the resulting geometric pattern
Predict what happens as more domains are added

scenes.brief_purpose: Present and name the five fundamental geometries that result from 2 through 6 electron domains around a central atom. Students see each geometry built up incrementally and hear/read its name and identifying features.
key_visuals: Five 3D molecular geometry models displayed side by side or in sequence: linear (2 domains), trigonal planar (3), tetrahedral (4), trigonal bipyramidal (5), octahedral (6)
Central atom and electron domains clearly marked
Labeled bond angles for each geometry (180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°/120°, 90°)
Brief descriptive text for each shape
student_actions: Identify each geometry as it is presented
Note the characteristic bond angles and domain positions
Rotate and inspect each 3D model from different angles
Match the geometry names to the structures

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pairs in Tetrahedral and Trigonal Planar Bases
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how lone pairs modify the electron-domain geometry within the tetrahedral and trigonal planar cases. Students manipulate the position of one or more lone pairs and observe how molecular geometry changes (e.g., tetrahedral → trigonal pyramidal or bent).
key_visuals: Tetrahedral electron-domain geometry with 4 domains, where one can be toggled as a lone pair
Trigonal planar electron-domain geometry with 3 domains, where one or two can be toggled as lone pairs
Real-time visual feedback showing bonding pairs vs. lone pairs in different colors or styles
Resulting molecular geometries labeled: trigonal pyramidal (3 bonding + 1 lone in tetrahedral base), bent (2 bonding + 2 lone in tetrahedral base), bent (2 bonding + 1 lone in trigonal planar base)
student_actions: Toggle a domain between 'bonding pair' and 'lone pair' status
Observe how the 3D structure reorganizes or visually changes
Count bonding pairs and lone pairs to determine molecular geometry
Predict and confirm the names of resulting geometries

scenes.scene_name: Lone Pairs in Trigonal Bipyramidal Geometry
scenes.brief_purpose: Explore how lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry occupy equatorial positions preferentially to minimize repulsion. Students add lone pairs and see the molecular geometry change to seesaw, T-shaped, or linear.
key_visuals: Trigonal bipyramidal electron-domain geometry (5 domains: 3 equatorial, 2 axial)
Visual distinction between axial and equatorial positions (color, label, or position relative to center)
One or two domains can be converted to lone pairs
Resulting molecular geometries: seesaw (1 lone pair equatorial), T-shaped (2 lone pairs equatorial), linear (3 lone pairs equatorial with 2 bonding pairs axial)
student_actions: Add a lone pair to the equatorial position and observe the resulting geometry
Predict where a second lone pair will occupy and confirm by toggling
Name the resulting molecular geometries (seesaw, T-shaped, linear)
Observe that axial positions are less favorable for lone pairs due to higher repulsion

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how lone pairs in octahedral electron-domain geometry lead to square pyramidal and square planar molecular geometries. Students manipulate lone-pair positions and see the molecular shape change.
key_visuals: Octahedral electron-domain geometry (6 domains arranged at corners of cube)
One or two domains can be toggled as lone pairs
Resulting molecular geometries: square pyramidal (1 lone pair), square planar (2 lone pairs opposite each other)
Labels and colors distinguishing bonding pairs from lone pairs
student_actions: Toggle one domain to a lone pair and observe square pyramidal geometry
Add a second lone pair opposite the first to form square planar geometry
Rotate the 3D model to confirm the geometric arrangement
Name each resulting molecular geometry

scenes.brief_purpose: Explain quantitatively why lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, causing deviations from ideal bond angles. Students compare idealized angles (tetrahedral = 109.5°, trigonal planar = 120°) to observed angles in molecules with lone pairs.
key_visuals: Side-by-side comparison: methane (CH4, tetrahedral, all bonding pairs) vs. water (H2O, bent, 2 lone pairs)
Angle measurement tool or overlay showing 109.5° in methane and ~104.5° in water
Ammonia (NH3, trigonal pyramidal) with measured bond angle ~107°
Simple explanation or visual metaphor showing lone pairs occupying more angular space than bonding pairs
student_actions: Measure bond angles in provided molecular structures using an AR measurement tool
Compare observed angles to idealized angles for the electron-domain geometry
Explain why water's H–O–H angle is smaller than tetrahedral
Predict bond angles in other molecules based on lone-pair effects

scenes.brief_purpose: Apply VSEPR predictions to real molecules and confirm the theory against observed 3D structures. Students analyze Lewis structures and predict geometry, then compare to known experimental structures.
key_visuals: Lewis structures for water (H2O), ammonia (NH3), methane (CH4), phosphorus pentafluoride (PF5), sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), xenon tetrafluoride (XeF4)
Predicted 3D structures based on VSEPR
Experimental/known 3D structures displayed alongside predictions
Bond lengths and angles labeled where relevant
student_actions: Select a Lewis structure and count electron domains around the central atom
Predict the electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and bond angles
View the experimental structure and confirm the prediction
Analyze which molecules have lone pairs and how they affect the geometry
Reflect on successful predictions and any deviations

scenes.brief_purpose: Consolidate learning by having students independently predict molecular geometry from a Lewis structure, then build the 3D structure by placing electron domains and lone pairs in an AR builder tool.
key_visuals: A new Lewis structure presented (e.g., CHCl3, PCl5, SF5-, ClF3)
An interactive 3D canvas with a central atom and draggable electron-domain 'tiles' or 'spheres'
Real-time feedback showing the geometry as domains are positioned
Comparison to correct answer at the end of the challenge
student_actions: Analyze a provided Lewis structure to determine electron domains and lone pairs
Manually place bonding and lone-pair domains around the central atom in 3D space
Allow the system to show the minimum-repulsion configuration or manually arrange domains
Compare their constructed geometry to the correct answer
Receive feedback on accuracy and reflect on mistakes
